items.text: SEASON 9 · EPISODE 9 · DRAFT  The board room · Odile, Solveig, Raffa, Dario, Tamsin, Kit, Maya and a board member · Level L5 · Advanced support (formulas on request)  The board wants the season reviewed: who owned the accounts, who approved them, why nobody removed them. And somebody wants a name for the report.  ⚑ RV-170: funding and risk acceptance are the owner’s. RV-172: figures illustrative. Some choices run on a clock.

items.title: The Review
items.stakes: The board wants to know who owned the integrator's accounts, who approved them, and why nobody removed them. And somebody wants a name.
items.reward: Every finding with an owner, every fix funded or accepted in writing — and nobody made the scapegoat.

objectives.text: Find how many findings had an owner
Spend the board's money by risk
Decide what you say when they want a name
Decide what happens to what isn't funded

items.rumor: The finding is the gap between two owners.

items.title: Everyone's gap, nobody's job.
items.body: Maya's table has a column headed ‘owner before this season’. Seven of nine cells hold a dash. The integrator thought the venue would remove its accounts at handover; the venue thought the integrator had. Security was never part of commissioning. The emergency templates were the old general manager's idea and nobody's system. Every failure this season lived in the space between two people who each thought it was the other's.
items.label: Test: the share with an owner — and why the account survived.

items.sub: Advanced · the skill behind this chapter

items.alt: A teaching moment: Odile and Maya beside a board. Nine findings this season. How many had a named owner before we started? Two. Seven of nine — seventy-eight percent — sat between two people who each thought it was the other's. Then the review is about the gaps, not the people. Score them, own them, fund them.

items.text: 📙 ON REQUEST · ADVANCED  Terms   Blameless review   RACI   Risk register   Risk acceptance   If you need it   ƒ Ask for the formula · Risk score   ƒ FORMULA · Risk score  R = L × I   L  likelihood, 1 (rare) to 5 (almost certain)  I  impact, 1 (minor) to 5 (severe)  R  risk score, 1 to 25      ƒ Ask for the formula · Percentage   ƒ FORMULA · Percentage  % = part ÷ whole × 100   part  the piece you are measuring  whole  everything it is part of

items.title: The name they wanted.
items.body: Halfway through, a board member stops the meeting. He has found the signage handover acceptance: ‘Template library accepted — K.O.’ “So it was Kit.” Two lines below on the same page: ‘Commissioning record reviewed — M.’ Neither line asked the person signing to open anything.

items.title: Holes that line up
items.body: In 1990 the psychologist James Reason described accidents in complex systems as holes lining up in slices of cheese: every layer of defence — design, procedure, training, supervision — has gaps, and harm gets through only when the gaps align. His point was that blaming the last person to touch something misses the other slices. Hospitals, airlines and power stations still teach it.

items.text: ✦ UX RULE #90 · AVERY'S LENS  Review the gaps, not the people  An organizational review asks what let each failure happen and who owns each fix — not who to blame.  Seven of nine findings sat between two people who each thought the other owned them. A name in the report would have fixed none of them.

items.text: FIELD NOTE —  Review blamelessly: what happened, what let it happen, who owned it before (% = part ÷ whole × 100 of findings with no owner). Give every system a RACI. Score fixes (R = L × I), fund them by risk inside the budget, and put what isn’t funded on the risk register, accepted in writing by its owner with a date to look again. When someone wants a name, say your own part first and fix the process.
REFLECTION (optional)  · Which problem in your work lives between two people who each think it’s the other’s?
